Bioluminescence is the production and emission of light by living organisms. It's a phenomenon found across various species, from tiny plankton to deep-sea creatures like anglerfish and giant squids. This natural light show occurs through a chemical reaction involving a light-emitting molecule called luciferin and an enzyme known as luciferase. When these substances interact with adenosine triphosphate (ATP), energy is released in the form of light.

One of the most captivating examples of bioluminescence can be seen in the depths of the ocean, where sunlight rarely penetrates. Here, creatures such as the anglerfish use bioluminescent lures to attract prey in complete darkness. The lantern fish, on the other hand, employ their glowing bodies for both camouflage and communication, allowing them to blend into the faint light filtering down from above or to signal to potential mates.
